blocks.html: Guests eat with their eyes first. Plating is not decoration added at the end: it is planned with the dish.

Principles chefs use: choose the plate to fit the food (size, shape, color); balance color (green, brown, red, white); add height without towers that topple; vary texture; leave negative space (clear plate) so the food has room; use odd numbers of small items (3 or 5 scallops) because they look natural; set a focal point; keep the rim clean. Many cooks picture the plate as a clock: protein near 6 o'clock (in front of the guest), starch at 10 or 11, vegetable at 2.

blocks.name: cu-plate
blocks.cap: Drag the parts onto the plate. Toggle the grid and the clock, and read the notes on balance and space.

blocks.html: A full plate looks crowded and hides the main item. Clear space frames the food the way a mat frames a picture. Odd groups are easier for the eye to see as one group; even groups pair off and look like rows.

blocks.title: Fix it
blocks.q: Four scallops lined up across the center of a crowded plate, with sauce up to the rim.
steps: Use three or five, grouped off-center.
Leave clear space; wipe the rim.
blocks.a: Three or five scallops off-center, more clear space, a clean rim.

blocks.html: Plating every dish as a tall tower. It looks dated and falls over on the way to the table.

🏠 Practice at home

  • Plate the same dinner four ways: crowded center, classic clock, off-center line, and a tall stack. Photograph each from above and from the guest's side, and pick the best.
  • Wipe every rim with a damp towel before the plate leaves your hands.

blocks.html: Sauce and garnish finish a plate. Done well, they add taste and texture as well as looks.

Sauce: a pool under the food (keeps crisp tops crisp), a drizzle or line, dots from a squeeze bottle, a swoosh or spoon drag, or poured at the table. Garnish rules: every garnish is edible, belongs to the dish (an ingredient or a natural partner), adds something (color, crunch, freshness), and is placed with care. A sprig of parsley on every plate is a habit, not a garnish.

items: Put sauce under or beside crisp food, not over it.
Use squeeze bottles for dots and lines; warm the sauce first so it flows.
For a spoon swoosh: place a spoonful, then drag the back of the spoon through it in one confident motion.
Garnish with something from the dish: a few of the herbs used in it, a crisp shard of the skin, a little of the vegetable raw.

blocks.html: Sauce poured over a crisp chicken skin softens it in a minute. Pooling it underneath keeps both textures.

blocks.title: Edible?
blocks.q: A rosemary branch laid across a plate of lamb as decoration.
steps: Use a few leaves, or rosemary oil, instead.
blocks.a: Not a good garnish; use something the guest can eat.

blocks.html: Garnish that tastes of nothing to do with the dish.

🏠 Practice at home

  • Practice sauce work on a plate with ketchup or yogurt: ten dots of the same size, a straight line, a spoon swoosh. Wipe and repeat until they look the same every time.

Each fork, knife, glass and plate on a formal table has a place, and the places follow a few simple rules.

Forks on the left, knives and spoons on the right, knife blades facing the plate. Guests use utensils from the outside in, one set per course. Glasses stand above the knives (water glass closest to the knife tip, wine glasses to its right). The bread plate sits at the upper left with its butter knife. Dessert spoon and fork lie above the plate. The napkin goes on the plate or to the left of the forks.

blocks.name: cu-setting
blocks.cap: Click any item to see what it is for and when it is used.

blocks.html: An easy memory trick: make OK signs with both hands. The left hand makes a "b" (bread, on the left); the right makes a "d" (drinks, on the right). In service, plates are often set down from the guest's left and cleared from the right, and drinks served from the right, though customs vary by restaurant.

head: Item
What it is for
rows: The salad course; outside left if salad comes first
A fish course: the fish knife has a broad, dull blade for lifting flesh off bones
Outside right when soup comes first
The only fork placed on the right, outside the spoons
To the right of the water glass, in the order used
Above the plate (spoon handle to the right, fork handle to the left)

blocks.title: Which fork first?
blocks.q: A dinner has a salad course, then a main course. Two forks lie to the left of the plate.

blocks.html: Grabbing the bread plate on your right. Solids on the left, liquids on the right.

🏠 Practice at home

  • Set a formal place setting for a four-course dinner (soup, fish, main, dessert) using what you have. Check it against the picture.

A tasting menu is many small courses chosen by the chef, served in an order that tells a story from first bite to last. It's how many fine-dining kitchens show what they can do.

A common modern order: an amuse-bouche (one bite, the chef's welcome); cold or raw dishes and lighter vegetables; a soup or seafood; a fish course; a richer meat course; often cheese; a pre-dessert (something light and cleansing, such as a sorbet); dessert; and mignardises (small sweets) with coffee. Courses move from light to rich, delicate to bold, savory to sweet.

head: Course
Typical size
rows: About 2 to 3 ounces of the main item each
One or two small pieces each
blocks.cap: Portions shrink so that 8 to 12 courses make a satisfying meal, not too much

blocks.html: A tasting menu works like a piece of music: changes in temperature, texture and intensity keep guests interested, and the order protects delicate flavors from being drowned by bold ones that came before.

blocks.title: Total protein
blocks.q: A tasting menu has four savory courses with about 2.5 ounces of protein each. How much in all per guest?

blocks.html: Serving full-size portions. Guests are full halfway through.

🏠 Practice at home

  • Write a seven-course tasting menu from dishes in this ladder. Check it moves from light to rich and that no two courses in a row share a main ingredient or method.

blocks.html: The same food can reach the table in different ways. Each style asks different things of the kitchen and the servers.

American (plated) service: food is plated in the kitchen and carried out; most restaurants work this way. Russian service (service à la russe): courses served one after another, presented on platters and served onto each guest's plate by a server. French service in restaurants (guéridon service): dishes finished, carved, flambéed or dressed on a cart beside the table. Family style: platters set on the table for guests to pass. English service: the host carves or serves at the table.

In history, "service à la française" meant something else: many dishes set on the table at once, which guests helped themselves to. In the 1800s Russian service, with courses one after another, replaced it in Europe, and that is the ancestor of the course-by-course meal we know.

blocks.title: Name the style
blocks.q: A server carves a duck and flambés crêpes on a cart beside the table.
steps: Finishing at a cart by the table.

blocks.html: Thinking family style is less work for the kitchen. The kitchen still cooks every dish; it just leaves on platters.

🏠 Practice at home

  • Serve one dinner at home family style and the next plated. Note how the timing and the number of dishes changed.

During service the pass is the kitchen's command center. One person, the expediter (or the chef), reads the tickets and calls the orders; the stations answer and cook.

How a ticket moves: the order comes in and the expediter calls it ("Ordering: two salmon, one steak medium-rare"); stations answer "heard" (or "yes, chef"). When it's time, the expediter fires the course ("Fire table 12"), and every station times its part to finish together. Plates come to the pass, the expediter checks each one (temperature, look, the right dish), wipes rims, and sends them with servers.

items: "All day" gives the total of one item on all open tickets: "four salmon all day".
"Walking in" or "hands" calls a server to carry plates.

blocks.html: Different dishes take different times: a steak needs 12 minutes, a salad one. The expediter fires each part so it all lands at the pass at the same moment, and the table gets everything hot and fresh together.

blocks.title: All day
blocks.q: Open tickets: table 3 has 2 salmon; table 7 has 1 salmon; table 9 has 3 salmon. How many salmon all day?

blocks.html: Starting a dish when the ticket arrives rather than when it's fired.

🏠 Practice at home

  • Cook a three-dish dinner with one person calling the orders and firing each dish. Practice answering "heard" and calling "behind" and "hot".
